opus-5.5.text:
I think the most interesting thing that comparison shows is that compute is not a substitute for intelligence, but it is a lever you can pull. When you put the constrained track next to the less constrained one, you see that throwing many orders of magnitude more compute at the problem does buy you something. You can sample more programs, search longer, and run bigger models at test time. But the returns are surprisingly modest relative to the cost. You're paying exponentially more for incremental gains.

That's exactly what you'd expect if the bottleneck is not raw processing but the quality of the abstractions the system brings to a new task. If you don't have the right building blocks, a brute-force search over a combinatorial space gets very expensive very fast. More compute lets you dig a bit deeper into that space, but it doesn't change its shape.

So for me the takeaway is that efficiency has to be part of how we define intelligence. If you can solve a task by spending a million dollars of compute on it, that tells you something, but it's not the same as solving it the way a human does, with a few examples and very little energy. Intelligence is about how efficiently you turn prior knowledge and experience into skill on something novel. The constrained track forces you to confront that directly. You can't hide a lack of generalization behind scale.

The other thing I'd point out is that the approaches doing well under tight budgets tend to be the more interesting ones scientifically. They combine learned intuition, which narrows down where to look, with explicit search or program synthesis, which actually verifies and composes solutions. That hybrid seems to be where progress comes from, rather than simply scaling one ingredient. If you only look at the high-compute results, it's easy to mistake spending for understanding.

r001.rationale: The response says much more compute brings modest incremental gains, but it does not state that the tracks achieved approximately the same scores.

r002.rationale: It identifies the quality of abstractions and a hybrid intuition-plus-search approach as ways to make progress under tight compute budgets, communicating that better approaches improve compute efficiency.

r003.rationale: It says brute-force search becomes expensive and that more compute lets systems search deeper, but does not claim unlimited compute could solve ARC.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the comparison is one of the most informative things that came out of running the prize, honestly. We essentially ran a natural experiment. On one side you had the Kaggle track, where you're constrained to something like twelve hours on a couple of GPUs with no internet access, and on the other side you had the public leaderboard, where frontier labs could throw essentially unlimited test-time compute at the problem. And the first takeaway is simply that the gap between those two settings was enormous. You could get scores on the high-compute track that were many times what the best Kaggle entries achieved, and the difference was not a difference in ideas. It was a difference in how much search you could afford to do per task.

That tells you something important about what these systems are actually doing. If an approach gets dramatically better the more samples you draw, the more chains of thought you run, the more programs you generate and verify, then what you're looking at is not a system that has the knowledge and is retrieving it. It's a system doing a search over possible solutions, where the quality of the prior is what determines how expensive that search is. And ARC tasks are specifically designed so that the prior you get from memorizing the internet is not very useful, so you end up paying a lot in search to compensate.

The second takeaway is that this is why I've insisted on efficiency being part of the definition of intelligence, rather than just raw score. If you can solve a task with a million dollars of compute, that's a fact about your budget, not a fact about your intelligence. A human solves these tasks in a few seconds with a brain that runs on about twenty watts. So when people point at a high score on the unconstrained track and say "ARC is solved," I think they're missing the point. The meaningful question is the score per unit of resource, and on that axis the gap between the best systems and a human is still very wide.

And the third thing, which I find encouraging rather than discouraging, is that the ideas that worked well under tight constraints are actually the more interesting ones scientifically. When you can't brute force, you're forced to do something structural: test-time training, program synthesis guided by a learned model, combining symbolic search with a neural prior. Those approaches are telling us something about what a genuine solution looks like. The unconstrained track tells us how far you can push the current paradigm with money. The constrained track tells us what the next paradigm might need to be. I care much more about the second question.

r001.rationale: The response says the high-compute track scored many times more than the best Kaggle entries, directly contradicting approximately equal scores.

r002.rationale: It says the score gap came from how much search compute was available and praises structural approaches, but does not state that better ideas make a given amount of compute more effective.

r003.rationale: The response describes search and brute force as ways to push the current paradigm, but does not say unlimited compute could solve ARC through brute-force search.

astra-6.text:
The interesting thing is that you can trade efficiency for compute, at least to some extent. You can take an approach that is relatively inefficient and push its performance higher by spending much more on search or adaptation at test time. But that doesn’t necessarily mean you’ve found a more general solution.

So when I compare the tracks, I’m interested in the relationship between performance and the resources required to achieve it. If two systems achieve similar scores, but one uses dramatically less compute, that’s a meaningful difference. The more efficient system may have a better way of representing the problem or finding the right abstraction.

This is central to what ARC is trying to measure: how efficiently you can acquire a new skill when confronted with something unfamiliar. A score alone doesn’t tell you the whole story. You want to look at the score alongside the compute budget, the prior knowledge, and the amount of task-specific engineering. The lower-budget track makes those questions harder to ignore.

r001.rationale: The response describes similar scores at different compute levels conditionally, but does not state that the actual high- and low-budget ARC Prize tracks achieved approximately the same scores.

r002.rationale: It says a system with a better representation or abstraction may achieve a similar score using dramatically less compute, communicating that better ideas make compute more effective.

r003.rationale: The response mentions spending more compute on search or test-time adaptation, but does not say unlimited compute could solve ARC through brute-force search.

sol-6.1.text:
What I take away is that we should distinguish the intelligence of a system from the amount of computation we spend running it. If you give one approach a much larger budget, it can explore more hypotheses, generate more candidate programs, and verify more solutions. That can improve its score substantially, but the score alone doesn’t tell you how efficiently it’s adapting to novelty.

So I’m interested in the relationship between performance and compute. Can you reach the same level of performance with a hundred times less computation? Can you solve a new task with very little experience? Those are meaningful advances, even if they don’t produce the highest absolute score.

The tracks give us different views of that relationship. A large budget helps us explore what’s possible; a constrained budget puts pressure on the quality of the method. You want both, but you shouldn’t collapse them into a single claim about how intelligent a system is.

r002.rationale: It emphasizes performance per unit of compute and method quality, but does not state that better ideas make a given compute budget more effective.
